paper.title: When the Floodgates Open: “Northern” Firms’ Response to Removal of Trade Quotas on Chinese Goods
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed beyond the following: …

registers.role: outcomes (turnover, value added, FTE employment, capital, investment, intangible assets, total assets) and sample frame
outcomes (head-count employment, occupation and education composition, hourly wages) and worker characteristics
variables_mentioned: DISCO-88 occupation code of the position an employee holds within a firm

registers.role: treatment (firm product portfolios) and outcomes (dropped and new products)
variables_mentioned: 10-digit product-firm-year-level sales of domestically produced products

registers.name_in_paper: international trade dataset compiled from Danish customs records
registers.role: treatment (MFA quota goods imported/produced by firms), import and export outcomes, sample frame for the product-level analysis

registers.name_in_paper: SIGL (Systeme Integre de Gestion de Licenses) database, European Commission
registers.role: treatment definition: MFA quota categories mapped to CN 8-digit products
variables_mentioned: 163 grouped quota categories defined by the European Union

linkages: Key to matching the datasets is a unique ID for each firm common to all datasets
Employee characteristics compiled from person-level data (IDA) with matched employer code, linked to firm accounting data
Firms that produce the MFA goods are identified using firm IDs, which are reported as part of the domestic and foreign sales datasets
EU quota categories mapped to CN 8-digit products based on Combined Nomenclature 1999, linked across years with European Commission-Eurostat correspondence tables (CN-1995 to CN-2007)

sample.universe: Danish textile and clothing (T&C) manufacturing firms and their employees, 1995-2007; plus Danish transaction-level T&C imports at CN 8-digit product level
sample.unit_of_observation: firm-year (main analysis), worker-year (wage analysis), CN-8 product x country x year and CN-8 product x year (trade analysis)
selection_rules: Firm accounting data contains all firms that employ at least 0.5 full-time equivalent labor
The person-level dataset covers all people ages 15 to 70
After cleaning out firms with low-quality data, the final dataset is comprised of around 1,100 unique T&C firms between 1995 and 2007
Due to data cleaning procedures some of the very small firms (with single employees) and firms with multiple entry and exits are cleaned out from the final dataset
The treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999, before China's WTO accession, produced goods that were subject to MFA quotas for China
The domestic production dataset contains only manufacturing firms that have ten or more employees, so the treatment group may miss some very small firms that do not trade internationally
1995 is excluded from the occupation analysis because occupation classifications changed in 1996 (DISCO-88)
2007 is excluded from the education analysis because the 8-digit education variable is not available that year
The product-churning analysis is restricted to 1996-2004 because new products are not defined in 1995 and dropped products are not defined in 2005
The wage analysis only covers full-time employees
sample.n_observations: 7,274 firm-year observations in the largest firm-level regression; 102,561 worker-year observations in the worker-level wage regressions; 25,383 / 57,301 / 15,823 observations in the product-level import regressions
sample.n_individuals: around 1,100 unique T&C firms (1,034-1,155 firms per regression)

construction_notes: A total of 158 CN 8-digit products are identified as being the subject of 2002 quota abolishment for China (Phase I, II, and III); these goods constitute about 9 percent of both the total T&C import and export in Denmark during the sample period

A total of 389 CN 8-digit product categories are identified for which the quotas for China were permanently abolished in 2005; these constitute about 20 percent of total Danish T&C imports and 17 percent of total T&C export
Categories renegotiated with China after the 2005 surge (the 'Bra War' quotas, in force until 2008) are excluded from the MFAQ5 group

In 1999, 32 percent of the firms in the sample had at least one MFA good in their product portfolios; out of 640 firms in 1999, 112 were producing MFAQ2, 191 were producing MFAQ5 and 206 were producing either

Because the number of firms with no employees in a category increases for higher or more specialized occupation and education levels, the transformation 1 plus the number of employees is used when taking logarithms

Unit prices in the import regressions are not deflated; year-by-industry fixed effects are included instead to account for industry specific shocks including inflation rates and exchange rate variations
Three alternative exposure measures are constructed: MFAQProd99 (binary), MFAQProdShare99 (number of MFAQ products over total products in 1999) and MFAQRevShare99 (share of 1999 sales from MFAQ)
Industry n in the trade regressions denotes 'textile' or 'apparel', where product j belongs uniquely to one of them

claims.statement: The abolishment of the MFA quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's WTO accession (Dum02_t x China_k) raises log quantity for imports of MFA quota goods (Table 1, Panel A. MFAQ2 Products (1995-2007), col (1)).

register_source.value: Danish customs records (transaction-level import dataset 1995-2007 aggregated to CN-8 product x country x year), Statistics Denmark

definition.value: Interaction in equation (1) of Dum02_t, a time dummy that takes value 1 on and after the year 2002 and zero otherwise, with China_k, an indicator for the exporting country being China; estimated on imports of MFAQ2 goods (the 158 CN-8 products whose Chinese quotas were abolished in January 2002 as Phases I-II-III of the ATC following China's WTO accession).

timing.value: quota abolishment in January 2002; imports observed annually 1995-2007

register_source.value: Danish customs records (transaction-level import dataset), Statistics Denmark

definition.value: ln X_jkt, the natural logarithm of the imported quantity of 8-digit good j coming from country k at year t; transaction-level import data 1995-2007 aggregated into country, CN-8 product and year level.

units.value: log points of log quantity, as a disproportionate post-2002 change relative to the comparison group

magnitude.interpretation: a more than five times disproportionate increase of the Chinese imports in the 2002 quota goods in comparison to imports from other countries of the same 8-digit goods

estimand.target_population: imports of MFA quota goods
estimand.time_horizon: average disproportionate change over the post-2002 years of the 1995-2007 sample; no event-time dynamics are estimated
estimand.formal_query: E[log quantity | do(Dum02_t x China_k=1)] - E[log quantity | do(Dum02_t x China_k=0)] for imports of MFA quota goods

population.description: Danish imports of the 158 CN 8-digit textile and clothing products that were the subject of the 2002 quota abolishment for China (Phases I, II and III), observed at exporting-country by CN-8 product by year level, 1995-2007. These goods constitute about 9 percent of both the total T&C import and export in Denmark during the sample period.
subgroups_defined: exporting country China versus other exporters of the same CN-8 goods
population.selection: Transaction-level Danish customs import records for textile and clothing goods, restricted to MFAQ2 products and aggregated to CN-8 product by country by year

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO: Phases I-III removed in January 2002 and Phase IV in January 2005, compared with the same CN-8 goods imported from other countries / with non-quota goods.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, imports from China (or of quota goods) would have followed the same path as imports of the same CN-8 goods from other countries (or of non-quota goods), conditional on product-by-country and year-by-industry fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Country-by-product fixed effects are included to control for changes at the extensive margin and year-by-industry fixed effects to account for industry specific shocks including inflation rates and exchange rate variations; no pre-trend test is reported for Table 1 or Table 2.

key_assumptions.assumption: The timing and extent of the quota abolishment is exogenous to Danish import demand: it was driven by China's WTO accession and the ATC phase-out schedule, not by Danish market conditions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the empirical strategy directly utilizes the change in trade policy rather than relying on import measures that are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors.

key_assumptions.assumption: The measured unit-price change reflects the price of comparable goods rather than a change in product quality in response to quota relaxation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper concedes part of the unit price decline could be due to changes in the quality of the products, and cites Khandelwal, Schott, and Wei (2013), who find most of the decline was due to entry of more efficient Chinese firms rather than quality downgrading.

threats_discussed: Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors
Part of the unit price decline could be due to changes in the quality of the products in response to the relaxation of the quota restrictions
China may merely replace other developing-country import partners without significantly affecting prices
robustness_checks: Equation (2) re-estimated with a single dummy for all quota phases combined (Table 2, column 2)
the same product-level analysis conducted on Danish export data (online Appendix Table A-1)
unresolved_confounders: Part of the unit-price decline for Chinese goods could be due to changes in product quality rather than price competition

estimator.value: OLS with product-by-country and year-by-industry fixed effects (difference-in-differences on transaction-level import data)

estimation.specification: Equation (1), estimated on MFAQ2 imports (panel A) and separately on MFAQ5 imports (panel B) (coefficient on Dum02_t x China_k)
fixed_effects: year by industry (tau_t x nu_n), where industry n denotes 'textile' or 'apparel'
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered for each CN 8-digit product category and country pair; clustering only by country leads to smaller standard errors

source_table.value: Table 1, Panel A. MFAQ2 Products (1995-2007), col (1)

adjustment_set.label: year by industry (tau_t x nu_n), where industry n denotes 'textile' or 'apparel'

evidence.how: The treatment interaction switches on in 2002 and the estimation sample ends in 2007, so the single post-period coefficient averages the disproportionate change over 0 to 5 years after the quota removal; the paper estimates no event-time path.

value.as_printed: ln Xjkt = α0 + α1 Dum02t × Chinak + ck × πj + τt × νn + ϵjkt .
value.lhs: ln X_jkt (log imported quantity, or log unit price, of good j from country k in year t)
value.normalisation: Country-by-product fixed effects c_k x pi_j and year-by-industry fixed effects tau_t x nu_n absorb the levels; Dum02_t is zero before 2002 and one from 2002 on, so the pre-2002 non-China cell is the reference. Unit prices are not deflated.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: the same product-level analysis conducted on Danish export data (online Appendix Table A-1)

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors

register_source.value: Domestic production dataset and Danish customs records (product-firm-year sales), Statistics Denmark; quota categories from the European Commission SIGL database

definition.value: Difference-in-differences interaction of MFAQProd99_i -- an indicator taking value 1 if firm i produced any MFA quota good for China (MFAQ) in 1999, before China's WTO accession -- with Dum02_t, a time dummy equal to 1 on and after 2002 and zero otherwise. The treatment group is fixed at the 1999 product portfolio to prevent selection within the treatment group. Firm product portfolios are built from the domestic production (10-digit product-firm-year) and the international customs (CN 8-digit) datasets; the 158 CN-8 products subject to the 2002 (Phase I-II-III) abolishment and the 389 subject to the 2005 abolishment are identified from the EU SIGL licence database mapped to CN-1999.

timing.value: exposure measured in 1999; treatment switched on from 2002 onwards

register_source.value: Regnskabsdata (longitudinal firm accounting data), Statistics Denmark

definition.value: the logarithm of the total investment in physical assets

timing.value: firm-year, 1995-2007

units.value: log points of log investment, as a disproportionate post-2002 change relative to the comparison group

estimand.time_horizon: average disproportionate change over the post-2002 years of the 1995-2007 sample; no event-time dynamics are estimated
estimand.formal_query: E[log investment | do(MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t=1)] - E[log investment | do(MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t=0)] for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002

population.description: Danish textile and apparel manufacturing firms, 1995-2007; the final dataset comprises around 1,100 unique T&C firms with 43 percent of them in clothing and the rest in the textile industry (1,071 to 1,155 firms per column).
subgroups_defined: firms producing MFA quota goods in 1999 versus other T&C manufacturers
intensity of 1999 MFAQ product share

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

falsification.condition: A significant disproportionate impact on the treated firms before 2002 -- in particular from the 1995 and 1998 MFA quota phases, from which China did not benefit -- would invalidate the empirical approach; the paper reports that there was no significant impact until 2002.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: share of college educated employees and wage share of college educated employees, and average education and experience within occupation groups (online Appendix Table A-3)

anchor_quote.text: of the low-wage competition on the number of employees with T&C-related technical design education is positive and significant.

claims.statement: Intensified Chinese low-wage competition from the MFA quota abolishment, measured by MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t raises log of avg. hourly wage for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002 (Table 5, col (1)).

register_source.value: Domestic production dataset and Danish customs records (product-firm-year sales), Statistics Denmark; quota categories from the European Commission SIGL database

definition.value: Difference-in-differences interaction of MFAQProd99_i -- an indicator taking value 1 if firm i produced any MFA quota good for China (MFAQ) in 1999, before China's WTO accession -- with Dum02_t, a time dummy equal to 1 on and after 2002 and zero otherwise. The treatment group is fixed at the 1999 product portfolio to prevent selection within the treatment group. Firm product portfolios are built from the domestic production (10-digit product-firm-year) and the international customs (CN 8-digit) datasets; the 158 CN-8 products subject to the 2002 (Phase I-II-III) abolishment and the 389 subject to the 2005 abolishment are identified from the EU SIGL licence database mapped to CN-1999.

timing.value: exposure measured in 1999; treatment switched on from 2002 onwards

register_source.value: Persondata (IDA), Statistics Denmark

definition.value: the logarithm of average hourly wages within firms; the analysis only covers full-time employees

timing.value: firm-year, 1996-2006

units.value: log points of log of avg. hourly wage, as a disproportionate post-2002 change relative to the comparison group

estimand.target_population: Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002
estimand.time_horizon: average disproportionate change over the post-2002 years of the 1996-2006 sample; no event-time dynamics are estimated
estimand.formal_query: E[log of avg. hourly wage | do(MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t=1)] - E[log of avg. hourly wage | do(MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t=0)] for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002

population.description: Danish textile and apparel industry firms, 1996-2006 (1,041 firms, 5,998 firm-year observations); the analysis only covers full-time employees.
subgroups_defined: firms producing MFA quota goods in 1999 versus other T&C manufacturers
population.selection: Firm-level averages of hourly wages of full-time employees, from IDA matched to the firm accounting data

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

threats_discussed: Serial correlation in the dependent variables in a DID setting with long time series may cause underestimation of standard errors
Selection within the treatment group if firms drop high-Chinese-advantage products after 2002 (addressed by fixing the treatment group at 1999)
Spillovers from MFA producers onto other T&C and non-T&C firms, which the approach does not address
Very small firms that do not trade internationally may be missing from the treatment group, which may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Imported input / offshoring effects on treated firms that both produce and import MFA quota goods, which would mute the measured competition effect
Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors
robustness_checks: Aggregating the data into two periods (pre- and post-WTO) to address serial correlation, following Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) (online Appendix Tables A-4 to A-6)
Alternative pre-event dates for defining the treatment group, such as 1995 or 1998, and defining treatment as producing any MFAQ in any year until 1999
Placebo check on the 1995 and 1998 quota phases, from which China did not benefit (online Appendix Table A-7)
Three alternative exposure measures: MFAQProd99, MFAQProdShare99 and MFAQRevShare99
Count-data nonlinear estimator without the log(1+x) transformation for occupation and education employee counts
Treating the 2002 and 2005 quota removals separately (online Appendix)
Two-stage least squares with a firm-specific Chinese import measure instrumented with the quota dummies (online Appendix)
Worker fixed effects in the wage regressions and a continuous treatment measure (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)
unresolved_confounders: Potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms are not addressed
Very small firms absent from the treatment group may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Part of the unit-price decline for Chinese goods could be due to changes in product quality rather than price competition

estimator.value: OLS difference-in-differences with fixed effects

estimation.specification: Equation (3) at the firm level (column 1) and at the worker level (columns 2-8) (coefficient on MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t)
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered for firms

mediators_claimed: selection within firms, since competition imposed lay-offs are concentrated among relatively less skilled employees
benefits to producer-importers from their own imports of MFA quota goods, and offshoring of base-level jobs raising home productivity
organizational change, including flattening of hierarchies

evidence.how: The treatment interaction switches on in 2002 and the estimation sample ends in 2006, so the single post-period coefficient averages the disproportionate change over 0 to 4 years after the quota removal; the paper estimates no event-time path.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

subgroups_defined: occupation categories (unspecified, auxiliary, base level, professional, executives)
education categories (below high school, vocational, college and above)
population.selection: Worker-year records from IDA restricted to full-time employees of T&C firms

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

threats_discussed: Serial correlation in the dependent variables in a DID setting with long time series may cause underestimation of standard errors
Selection within the treatment group if firms drop high-Chinese-advantage products after 2002 (addressed by fixing the treatment group at 1999)
Spillovers from MFA producers onto other T&C and non-T&C firms, which the approach does not address
Very small firms that do not trade internationally may be missing from the treatment group, which may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Imported input / offshoring effects on treated firms that both produce and import MFA quota goods, which would mute the measured competition effect
Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors
robustness_checks: Aggregating the data into two periods (pre- and post-WTO) to address serial correlation, following Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) (online Appendix Tables A-4 to A-6)
Alternative pre-event dates for defining the treatment group, such as 1995 or 1998, and defining treatment as producing any MFAQ in any year until 1999
Placebo check on the 1995 and 1998 quota phases, from which China did not benefit (online Appendix Table A-7)
Three alternative exposure measures: MFAQProd99, MFAQProdShare99 and MFAQRevShare99
Count-data nonlinear estimator without the log(1+x) transformation for occupation and education employee counts
Treating the 2002 and 2005 quota removals separately (online Appendix)
Two-stage least squares with a firm-specific Chinese import measure instrumented with the quota dummies (online Appendix)
Worker fixed effects in the wage regressions and a continuous treatment measure (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)
unresolved_confounders: Potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms are not addressed
Very small firms absent from the treatment group may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Part of the unit-price decline for Chinese goods could be due to changes in product quality rather than price competition

estimator.value: OLS difference-in-differences with fixed effects

estimation.specification: Equation (3) at the firm level (column 1) and at the worker level (columns 2-8) (coefficient on MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t x executives)
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered for firms

mediators_claimed: selection within firms, since competition imposed lay-offs are concentrated among relatively less skilled employees
benefits to producer-importers from their own imports of MFA quota goods, and offshoring of base-level jobs raising home productivity
organizational change, including flattening of hierarchies

heterogeneity.dimension: occupation / education category of the worker
heterogeneity.finding: The DID coefficient is fully interacted with occupation and education categories; the paper reports that the wage gain is accrued mostly among the professional occupations and among college-educated employees.

evidence.how: The treatment interaction switches on in 2002 and the estimation sample ends in 2006, so the single post-period coefficient averages the disproportionate change over 0 to 4 years after the quota removal; the paper estimates no event-time path.

value.as_printed: ln Xit = γ0 + γ1 Comp99i × Dum02t + δi + τt + ϵit .
value.lhs: ln X_it (log of the firm-level variable of interest for firm i in year t)
value.normalisation: Firm fixed effects delta_i and year fixed effects tau_t; Comp99_i is measured in 1999 and Dum02_t is zero before 2002, so the reference is the firm's own pre-2002 outcome net of the industry-wide year effect. For occupation and employee-count outcomes the dependent variable is the log of 1 plus the count.

value.claimed_domain: advanced country ('Northern') manufacturers facing Chinese or low-wage country competition
boundary_conditions: Danish textile and clothing industry
removal of MFA quotas following China's WTO accession
traditionally labor intensive manufacturing faced with stiff competition from low-wage countries
the general structure of the Danish labor market, with low cost of hiring and firing for firms and a high degree of unionization resulting in downwardly inflexible wages

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: the findings presented here on employment and wages support theirs, in that competition with low-wage countries mostly operates on the quantity margin within manufacturing sectors

falsification.condition: A significant disproportionate impact on the treated firms before 2002 -- in particular from the 1995 and 1998 MFA quota phases, from which China did not benefit -- would invalidate the empirical approach; the paper reports that there was no significant impact until 2002.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: wage results using the continuous treatment measures (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)

claims.statement: Intensified Chinese low-wage competition from the MFA quota abolishment, measured by MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t has no statistically significant effect on log of hourly wage of employees in the below high school category for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002; employees in the below high school category (Table 5, col (5)).

register_source.value: Domestic production dataset and Danish customs records (product-firm-year sales), Statistics Denmark; quota categories from the European Commission SIGL database

definition.value: Difference-in-differences interaction of MFAQProd99_i -- an indicator taking value 1 if firm i produced any MFA quota good for China (MFAQ) in 1999, before China's WTO accession -- with Dum02_t, a time dummy equal to 1 on and after 2002 and zero otherwise. The treatment group is fixed at the 1999 product portfolio to prevent selection within the treatment group. Firm product portfolios are built from the domestic production (10-digit product-firm-year) and the international customs (CN 8-digit) datasets; the 158 CN-8 products subject to the 2002 (Phase I-II-III) abolishment and the 389 subject to the 2005 abolishment are identified from the EU SIGL licence database mapped to CN-1999.

timing.value: exposure measured in 1999; treatment switched on from 2002 onwards

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: 1999 MFA-quota-good import status is not itself an endogenous response to the coming competition, so the triple-difference term isolates the import/offshoring channel rather than a differential propensity to adjust.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the triple difference by noting that producer-importers' presence in the treatment group would be expected to mute the negative effect, and measures import status in 1999; no test of the exogeneity of import status is reported.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

definition.value: Difference-in-differences interaction of MFAQImp99_i -- an indicator variable that shows if a firm imports any MFA quota goods in 1999 -- with Dum02_t, the dummy equal to 1 on and after 2002. timing.value: import status measured in 1999; post-period from 2002 onwards

timing.value: firm-year, 1995-2006

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: 1999 MFA-quota-good import status is not itself an endogenous response to the coming competition, so the triple-difference term isolates the import/offshoring channel rather than a differential propensity to adjust.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the triple difference by noting that producer-importers' presence in the treatment group would be expected to mute the negative effect, and measures import status in 1999; no test of the exogeneity of import status is reported.

threats_discussed: Serial correlation in the dependent variables in a DID setting with long time series may cause underestimation of standard errors

Spillovers from MFA producers onto other T&C and non-T&C firms, which the approach does not address

Imported input / offshoring effects on treated firms that both produce and import MFA quota goods, which would mute the measured competition effect
Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors

Placebo check on the 1995 and 1998 quota phases, from which China did not benefit (online Appendix Table A-7)
Three alternative exposure measures: MFAQProd99, MFAQProdShare99 and MFAQRevShare99
Count-data nonlinear estimator without the log(1+x) transformation for occupation and education employee counts
Treating the 2002 and 2005 quota removals separately (online Appendix)
Two-stage least squares with a firm-specific Chinese import measure instrumented with the quota dummies (online Appendix)
Worker fixed effects in the wage regressions and a continuous treatment measure (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)

Very small firms absent from the treatment group may cause underestimation of the effect of competition

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: 1999 MFA-quota-good import status is not itself an endogenous response to the coming competition, so the triple-difference term isolates the import/offshoring channel rather than a differential propensity to adjust.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the triple difference by noting that producer-importers' presence in the treatment group would be expected to mute the negative effect, and measures import status in 1999; no test of the exogeneity of import status is reported.

Imported input / offshoring effects on treated firms that both produce and import MFA quota goods, which would mute the measured competition effect
Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors

Placebo check on the 1995 and 1998 quota phases, from which China did not benefit (online Appendix Table A-7)
Three alternative exposure measures: MFAQProd99, MFAQProdShare99 and MFAQRevShare99
Count-data nonlinear estimator without the log(1+x) transformation for occupation and education employee counts
Treating the 2002 and 2005 quota removals separately (online Appendix)
Two-stage least squares with a firm-specific Chinese import measure instrumented with the quota dummies (online Appendix)
Worker fixed effects in the wage regressions and a continuous treatment measure (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: 1999 MFA-quota-good import status is not itself an endogenous response to the coming competition, so the triple-difference term isolates the import/offshoring channel rather than a differential propensity to adjust.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the triple difference by noting that producer-importers' presence in the treatment group would be expected to mute the negative effect, and measures import status in 1999; no test of the exogeneity of import status is reported.

definition.value: Triple-difference interaction in equation (4), with Comp99_i = MFAQProd99_i; it measures the variation in the dependent variable specific to MFAQ producers (relative to non-MFAQ producers) among MFAQ importers (relative to non MFAQ importers) in the years after the WTO accession of China, i.e. the extent to which importing MFA quota goods offsets the competition effect on MFAQ producers.

timing.value: production and import exposure measured in 1999; post-period from 2002 onwards

register_source.value: Persondata (IDA), Statistics Denmark

definition.value: the logarithm of the hourly wage at the worker level; the analysis only covers full-time employees

timing.value: worker-year, 1996-2006

units.value: log points of log of hourly wages, as a disproportionate post-2002 change relative to the comparison group

estimand.target_population: Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that both produced and imported MFA quota goods in 1999
estimand.time_horizon: average disproportionate change over the post-2002 years of the 1996-2006 sample; no event-time dynamics are estimated
estimand.formal_query: E[log of hourly wages | do(MFAQImp99_i x Comp99_i x Dum02_t=1)] - E[log of hourly wages | do(MFAQImp99_i x Comp99_i x Dum02_t=0)] for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that both produced and imported MFA quota goods in 1999

population.description: Full-time employees of Danish textile and apparel industry firms, 1996-2006: 102,561 worker-year observations in 1,034 firms.
subgroups_defined: occupation categories (unspecified, auxiliary, base level, professional, executives)
education categories (below high school, vocational, college and above)
population.selection: Worker-year records from IDA restricted to full-time employees of T&C firms

identification.source_of_variation: Abolishment of the Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on Chinese textile and clothing goods following China's accession to the WTO (Phases I-III removed January 2002, Phase IV January 2005); across-firm variation comes from whether a Danish T&C firm produced MFA quota goods in 1999, before the accession.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the MFA quota abolishment, firms that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 and other Danish textile and apparel manufacturers would have followed the same trend in the outcome, conditional on firm and year fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Aggregate trends in the industry are controlled for with year fixed effects and firm fixed effects absorb level differences; Table A-7 in the online Appendix reports year-by-year employment changes since 1995 for 1995 MFA producers and the paper states these confirm there was no significant impact until 2002.

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: firms did not adjust before 2002 in expectation of the quota removal, because there was a great deal of uncertainty about China's WTO membership and its timing during the 1990s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper documents recurring uncertainty about China's accession in contemporaneous press reports and states that the empirical strategy utilizes the uncertainty associated with the WTO accession of China; the Phase I and II removals of 1995 and 1998, from which China did not benefit, are used as a validation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the quota removal does not spill over from MFA quota goods producers onto the comparison group of other textile, clothing and non-T&C firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states outright that this empirical approach does not address potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms; no evidence is offered that they are absent.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects, exposure to the quota removal is unrelated to other determinants of the outcome; the shock to the competitive environment is exogenous because it was driven by China's WTO accession rather than by Danish demand or supply.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the strategy exploits the exogenous trade shock due to China's accession to the WTO and that firm fixed effects can be correlated with the regressors and thus further help to reduce the endogeneity concerns.

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment status is conditioned on the 1999 product portfolio, before China's WTO accession, so that endogenous product dropping after 2002 does not select the treatment group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states that to prevent biased results from such selection within the treatment group, the treatment group is set as those firms that in 1999 produced goods subject to MFA quotas; it notes the results are robust to using 1995 or 1998 instead.

key_assumptions.assumption: 1999 MFA-quota-good import status is not itself an endogenous response to the coming competition, so the triple-difference term isolates the import/offshoring channel rather than a differential propensity to adjust.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the triple difference by noting that producer-importers' presence in the treatment group would be expected to mute the negative effect, and measures import status in 1999; no test of the exogeneity of import status is reported.

threats_discussed: Serial correlation in the dependent variables in a DID setting with long time series may cause underestimation of standard errors
Selection within the treatment group if firms drop high-Chinese-advantage products after 2002 (addressed by fixing the treatment group at 1999)
Spillovers from MFA producers onto other T&C and non-T&C firms, which the approach does not address
Very small firms that do not trade internationally may be missing from the treatment group, which may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Imported input / offshoring effects on treated firms that both produce and import MFA quota goods, which would mute the measured competition effect
Import-based competition measures are potentially contaminated with domestic demand and supply factors
robustness_checks: Aggregating the data into two periods (pre- and post-WTO) to address serial correlation, following Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) (online Appendix Tables A-4 to A-6)
Alternative pre-event dates for defining the treatment group, such as 1995 or 1998, and defining treatment as producing any MFAQ in any year until 1999
Placebo check on the 1995 and 1998 quota phases, from which China did not benefit (online Appendix Table A-7)
Three alternative exposure measures: MFAQProd99, MFAQProdShare99 and MFAQRevShare99
Count-data nonlinear estimator without the log(1+x) transformation for occupation and education employee counts
Treating the 2002 and 2005 quota removals separately (online Appendix)
Two-stage least squares with a firm-specific Chinese import measure instrumented with the quota dummies (online Appendix)
Worker fixed effects in the wage regressions and a continuous treatment measure (online Appendix Tables A-8 and A-9)
unresolved_confounders: Potential spillovers from MFA producers on other T&C and non-T&C firms are not addressed
Very small firms absent from the treatment group may cause underestimation of the effect of competition
Part of the unit-price decline for Chinese goods could be due to changes in product quality rather than price competition

estimator.value: OLS triple-difference with firm and year fixed effects

estimation.specification: Equation (4), with Comp99_i = MFAQProd99_i (coefficient on MFAQImp99_i x Comp99_i x Dum02_t)
controls: worker characteristics: gender dummy, the logarithm of worker's age, and tenure
education dummies (below high school, college and above)
occupation dummies (auxiliary, base level, professional occupations and executives)
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered for firms

mediators_claimed: selection within firms, since competition imposed lay-offs are concentrated among relatively less skilled employees
benefits to producer-importers from their own imports of MFA quota goods, and offshoring of base-level jobs raising home productivity
organizational change, including flattening of hierarchies

heterogeneity.dimension: whether the MFAQ-producing firm also imported MFA quota goods in 1999
heterogeneity.finding: The triple difference coefficients are positive, showing that firms that were producing MFAQ are less (negatively) affected by the competition if they were also importing MFAQ.

ambiguities: The table prints a single asterisk (significant at the 10 percent level) although the ratio of the coefficient to its printed standard error exceeds two; transcribed exactly as printed.

evidence.how: The treatment interaction switches on in 2002 and the estimation sample ends in 2006, so the single post-period coefficient averages the disproportionate change over 0 to 4 years after the quota removal; the paper estimates no event-time path.

value.lhs: ln X_it (log of the firm-level or worker-level variable of interest)

The reference group is non-MFAQ-producing, non-MFAQ-importing firms before 2002.

boundary_conditions: Danish textile and clothing industry
removal of MFA quotas following China's WTO accession
traditionally labor intensive manufacturing faced with stiff competition from low-wage countries

The results support the findings of Hummels (2011) and are in line with Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg (2008), Caliendo and Rossi-Hansberg (2008), and Thesmar and Thoenig (2000).

claims.statement: Intensified Chinese low-wage competition from the MFA quota abolishment, measured by MFAQProd99_i x Dum02_t has no statistically significant effect on log of hourly wages for Danish textile and apparel manufacturers that produced MFA quota goods in 1999 (the treated firms), after 2002 (Table 6, Panel C., col (4)).

register_source.value: Domestic production dataset and Danish customs records (product-firm-year sales), Statistics Denmark; quota categories from the European Commission SIGL database

definition.value: Difference-in-differences interaction of MFAQProd99_i -- an indicator taking value 1 if firm i produced any MFA quota good for China (MFAQ) in 1999, before China's WTO accession -- with Dum02_t, a time dummy equal to 1 on and after 2002 and zero otherwise. The treatment group is fixed at the 1999 product portfolio to prevent selection within the treatment group. Firm product portfolios are built from the domestic production (10-digit product-firm-year) and the international customs (CN 8-digit) datasets; the 158 CN-8 products subject to the 2002 (Phase I-II-III) abolishment and the 389 subject to the 2005 abolishment are identified from the EU SIGL licence database mapped to CN-1999.

timing.value: exposure measured in 1999; treatment switched on from 2002 onwards
